overview.heading: How the T-Shirt Design Maker works
paragraphs: You describe the artwork, add a slogan if you want one, choose one of ten styles and say whether the shirt is dark or light. PiCraft draws the graphic on its own, with bold shapes and a limited palette that suit screen printing and direct-to-garment printing, and removes the background so only the artwork remains.
The shirt color matters because it changes the palette. On a dark shirt the design leans on light and bright colors, and on a light shirt it uses darker tones, so nothing disappears into the fabric.
You download a transparent PNG at 4500×5400 px, which is 15×18 inches at 300 DPI, plus a small preview. Upload the large file to your print-on-demand store or hand it to a local printer.

whatYouGet.title: 4500×5400 px transparent PNG
whatYouGet.description: A full-size print file at 300 DPI covering a 15×18 inch front print area, with no background to remove.

whatYouGet.title: A web preview
whatYouGet.description: A 1200×1440 px transparent PNG for product mockups, social posts and shop thumbnails.

whatYouGet.title: Palette matched to the shirt
whatYouGet.description: Choose dark or light and the colors are adjusted so the artwork keeps its contrast on that fabric.

whatYouGet.title: Ten print-friendly styles
whatYouGet.description: Vintage badge, streetwear, line art, tattoo and more, all with clean edges and flat color areas that print well.

whatYouGet.title: Slogan built into the design
whatYouGet.description: Add up to 40 characters and the text is integrated into the artwork instead of being pasted on top.

useCases.title: Print-on-demand stores
useCases.description: Create a design, upload the PNG to Merch on Demand, Printful, Printify or Redbubble, and list it without handling inventory.

useCases.title: Team, club and event shirts
useCases.description: Make a one-off design for a sports team, a family reunion, a fun run or a school event and hand the file to a local print shop.

useCases.title: Niche merchandise
useCases.description: Test small audiences, such as hobbies, jobs and inside jokes, with several designs before committing to one.

useCases.title: Creators and small brands
useCases.description: Turn a catchphrase or a mascot idea into merch your audience can buy, without hiring an illustrator for the first draft.

useCases.title: Gifts
useCases.description: Print a single shirt with a private joke or a pet-themed design, using any service that accepts a PNG.

tips.title: Pick the shirt color first
tips.description: Decide whether the design is for a dark or light shirt before you generate. Switching later means generating again, because the palette changes.

tips.title: Think of it as a chest graphic
tips.description: A single focal point, such as a badge, an animal or a landscape in a circle, looks better on fabric than a full scene.

tips.title: Keep the slogan short
tips.description: Two to five words print cleanly. Long sentences shrink until they are unreadable on a shirt.

tips.title: Choose a style that prints well
tips.description: Flat colors and thick outlines reproduce reliably. Fine textures and soft gradients can look muddy on some fabrics.

tips.title: Describe the subject and the mood
tips.description: "A camper van driving toward a mountain range inside a circle, calm and nostalgic" gives more direction than "camping shirt".

tips.title: Look at it on a mockup
tips.description: Place the PNG on a shirt photo or in your platform's mockup tool before publishing. It shows scale and contrast problems the flat file hides.

tips.title: Stay original
tips.description: Describe your own idea. Platforms take down listings that copy trademarks, logos, characters or other people's artwork.

styleGuide.heading: Choosing a shirt style
styleGuide.intro: The style decides the line work and the feeling of the graphic. These are the ten options and what each is good at.

items.title: Vintage badge
items.description: Circular or shield layouts with worn-in color. Best for outdoors, travel and local brands.

items.title: Streetwear
items.description: Bold type and graphic shapes with an urban feel. Best for slogans and limited drops.

items.title: Minimal line art
items.description: Thin single-color lines with lots of space. Best for subtle designs on light shirts.

items.title: Cute illustration
items.description: Friendly characters and soft shapes. Best for pets, kids and gifts.

items.title: Bold graphic
items.description: Large flat shapes and strong contrast. Best for team shirts and statements.

items.title: Japanese ink
items.description: Brush-stroke textures and calm composition. Best for nature and martial arts themes.

items.title: Grunge texture
items.description: Rough edges and a distressed finish. Best for music and rebellious slogans.

items.title: Geometric abstract
items.description: Clean shapes in a tight palette. Best for modern, design-minded shirts.

items.title: Retro sports
items.description: Varsity lettering and stripes. Best for clubs, leagues and humor with a jersey look.

items.title: Traditional tattoo
items.description: Heavy outlines and classic motifs such as roses, daggers and swallows. Best for bold, nostalgic art.

checklist.heading: Before you upload to a print service
items: Preview the PNG over both a dark and a light background to confirm the artwork holds up on your shirt color.
Read the slogan letter by letter and check it against what you typed.
Check your platform's current file rules for size, color space and file weight before uploading.
If your platform wants artwork trimmed to the edge of the design, crop away the transparent margin in your image editor first.
Look at the design on a mockup at real size to check scale and placement.
Search the slogan and the idea to make sure they are not a registered trademark or someone else's artwork.
Order one sample shirt before you promote a design to customers.

limits: The 4500×5400 px print file is upscaled from the generated design. Bold shapes print sharply, but fine detail will not look like vector art.
The PNG is flat. For a new color or a moved element, generate a new design.
Colors on screen and on fabric differ, and fabric type changes the result. A sample print is the only reliable check.
The maker designs front graphics. It does not produce mockups, back prints or all-over patterns.
Long text can come out with errors, so always proofread.
